title: Files, Documents, Images, and Search: How Applications Find Information
description: Not everything a product knows fits into rows and columns. Learn where files actually live, how a database record points at a file it cannot hold, and how an application chooses between filtering, keyword search, and semantic search to deliver the right information to an AI.

objectives.label: Distinguish structured, semi-structured, and unstructured information and why each changes the architecture
Explain how a database record about a file relates to the file itself in object storage
Match a retrieval question to the right tool: database filter, keyword search, or semantic search
Trace the pipeline that turns an uploaded document into information an AI can answer from

lessons.title: When facts stop fitting in tables

slides.title: The report does not fit in a row

blocks.text:
A nonprofit application tracks hundreds of community organizations. Name, city, category and active status fit a table perfectly. But each organization also has a 40-page annual report, photos, flyers and meeting recordings.

You cannot create a column called annual_report_paragraph_1. The question has changed from how do I organize facts to how do I organize knowledge.

Having access to a file is not the same thing as understanding its contents.

blocks.alt: Three kinds of information: a structured student record with named fields, a semi-structured JSON document whose fields can vary, and an unstructured PDF full of paragraphs and photos
blocks.caption: The system knows the shape of the first, half-knows the second, and receives the third as a file.
steps: Structured: student_id, name, county, graduation_year — the system knows exactly what each value means
Semi-structured: a JSON document whose fields can differ from record to record, like API payloads and logs
Unstructured: a PDF full of paragraphs, tables, photos and charts — it arrives as one file

blocks.text:
Structured information has named fields the system can filter. Semi-structured information, such as JSON logs, has fields that can vary from record to record.

Unstructured information arrives as a file. Names and dates may live inside a PDF, but until something extracts them, the application cannot address them as fields.

blocks.question: A scanned grant application arrives as one PDF. Which form of information is it?

options.label: Structured, because the application received it as a file
Unstructured, because the system receives one file and does not automatically understand the paragraphs inside
Semi-structured, because PDFs travel through APIs like JSON
Structured, because the document contains names and dates

blocks.explanation: The system receives the PDF as a file. Names and dates exist inside it, but the application cannot address them as fields the way it can address a student's county. Until something extracts structure, the document is unstructured information.

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: Having access to a file is not the same thing as understanding its contents.

blocks.alt: An application connected to three systems: a database holding structured facts, file storage holding the actual files, and a search index holding structures built for finding information
blocks.caption: These systems are not competing with each other. Each is optimized for a different kind of work, and a real product may use all three at once.
steps: Database: organization IDs, names, categories, permissions — facts the system can query
File storage: the actual PDFs, photos, videos and recordings
Search index: prepared structures that make information findable

blocks.text:
These systems are not competing. The database holds facts and permissions. Object storage holds the bytes. A search index holds structures prepared so finding information is fast.

A real product may use all three at once.

blocks.title: Maya uploads a report
steps: Maya uploads tulsa-youth-sports-annual-report-2026.pdf through the application.
The actual PDF goes into object storage at /files/organizations/381/reports/2026-report.pdf.
The database creates a document record: document_id 9127, organization_id 381, filename, document_type annual_report, uploaded_at.
The record also stores the storage_location pointing at the real file outside the database.
IDs, ownership, type and permissions live in the database; the bytes live in storage. The record is a relationship that crosses systems.

blocks.question: A user opens a document page and sees the PDF. What did the database contribute to that moment?

options.label: The PDF bytes themselves, stored in a documents table
The document's ID, owner, type and the location of the actual file in storage
A copy of every paragraph, for fast reading
Nothing — the file storage does all the work

blocks.explanation: The database stores facts about the file: who it belongs to, what type it is, and where the bytes live. The record is a relationship that crosses systems, pointing outside the database to the object that holds the file itself.

slides.title: What it is, versus the thing itself

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: The database helps the application know what the object is. Object storage holds the object itself.

blocks.alt: Three questions mapped to three retrieval tools: show active organizations in Tulsa goes to a database filter, find documents containing basketball goes to text search, and find programs for a teenager who enjoys sports goes to semantic search
blocks.caption: Different retrieval problems require different tools. Fast retrieval also requires preparation: an index is work done before the search so the search can be quick.
steps: "Show active organizations in Tulsa" → database filter: records whose fields match conditions
"Find documents containing basketball" → keyword search: scan the text of documents
"Find programs for a teenager who enjoys sports" → semantic search: match by meaning, not exact words
Pipelines combine them: filter by county and status first, then semantic-search within that smaller set

blocks.text:
Different retrieval problems need different tools. Named fields with exact values use a database filter. Exact words inside documents use keyword search. Similarity of meaning uses semantic search.

Pipelines often combine them: filter by county and status first, then search by meaning inside that smaller set.

slides.title: When the words do not match

blocks.text:
A user searches for opportunities for teenagers who enjoy sports. A perfect document says it organizes basketball leagues for students ages 14 to 18. Almost no words overlap, yet the meaning matches.

An embedding is a mathematical representation of meaning that lets a computer compare pieces of information by similarity. Searching on those representations is called semantic or vector search.

Semantic search does not replace filters for exact facts such as county or active status.

blocks.question: The product needs to find organizations in Oklahoma County that are currently active. Which retrieval tool fits?

options.label: Semantic search, because county and status are complicated ideas
Keyword search over every stored document
A database filter on the county and active fields
Ask the AI model to read every organization record

blocks.explanation: The question is about named fields with exact values, which is what a database filter is built for: precise, fast and predictable. Keyword and semantic search solve different problems — matching words inside documents and matching meaning — and would be slower and less precise here.

slides.title: Upload a PDF, ask a question

blocks.alt: A pipeline from an uploaded PDF through file storage, a document record, text extraction, chunking and indexing into a search system; later a user question triggers search and retrieval and the retrieved passages go to the AI, which generates an answer
blocks.caption: Find first, generate second — that order is the whole idea behind retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG.
steps: User uploads a PDF → file storage keeps the original
Database creates the document record
Text extraction reads the text out of the PDF
Chunking breaks the document into useful sections
Indexing prepares the sections for search
Later: a question triggers search and retrieval of the strongest passages
The AI receives the question plus the retrieved passages and generates the answer

blocks.text:
Find first, generate second. That order is retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG. A bad answer can be born long before the model: weak extraction, poor chunking, bad indexing, or bad retrieval all deliver the wrong passages.

Changing the prompt at the bottom of that pipeline may accomplish nothing if the wrong page never reached the model.

blocks.question: The PDF answers the user's question on page 187, but the AI answers wrongly and the prompt looks fine. What is a likely cause?

options.label: The AI model forgot how to read
The page was never extracted, was chunked badly, or retrieval returned the wrong sections
The database stored the PDF incorrectly
The user asked in the wrong language

blocks.explanation: A bad answer can be born long before the model: weak extraction, poor chunking, bad indexing or bad retrieval all deliver the wrong information to a perfectly fine model. Changing the prompt at the bottom of that pipeline may accomplish nothing.

slides.title: The right information at the right moment

blocks.title: Punchline
blocks.text: An AI model does not need to know everything. The surrounding system needs to deliver the right information at the right moment.
